subject: Historia 1a1
title: The world wars of the 20th century
sourceSummary: Causes of the First and Second World Wars, totalitarian ideologies, the course and consequences of the wars, the Holocaust in brief, and the founding of the UN.

questions.prompt: What structural factors, beyond the assassination in Sarajevo, allowed the First World War to break out?
questions.opener: Think about the arms race, the struggle for colonies, and the binding alliances between the great powers.
choices: France and Germany had agreed to divide up Europe
The League of Nations demanded that all countries go to war
Militarism, imperialist rivalry over colonies, and an alliance system that bound Europe's great powers together
All European countries were governed by the same government
questions.explanation: The assassination of Franz Ferdinand was only the triggering spark. The underlying structural causes were a prolonged arms race (militarism), rivalry over colonies and influence (imperialism), and the alliance system that drew the great powers into each other's conflicts. The League of Nations was not founded until after the war, in 1920.

questions.prompt: What was an important difference between the causes of the First and Second World Wars?
questions.opener: Think about whether the war grew out of a system of alliances, or out of a deliberate policy of conquest.
choices: The First World War grew out of alliances and great-power rivalry, while the Second World War was to a large extent driven by a deliberate policy of expansion by Nazi Germany and Japan
Both wars were caused solely by the same single event
The Second World War had no connection to the consequences of the First World War
The First World War was caused by the economic crisis of the 1930s
questions.explanation: The First World War was triggered in a relatively unplanned way through the chain reaction of the alliance system, while the Second World War was to a large extent driven by Nazi Germany's and Japan's deliberate pursuit of territorial expansion. At the same time the wars are connected: the harsh terms of the Treaty of Versailles contributed to the discontent that Nazism exploited.

questions.prompt: What characterises a totalitarian ideology, such as Nazism, fascism or Stalinist communism, compared with an ordinary dictatorship?
questions.opener: Think about how much of society and the individual's life the state seeks to control.
choices: A totalitarian state never interferes in citizens' private lives
A totalitarian state allows a free press and several political parties
A totalitarian state is governed solely through democratic elections without limitations
The state seeks to control virtually every part of society and the individual's life, often through propaganda, terror and a single permitted ideology
questions.explanation: Totalitarian states are characterised by power seeking total control — over politics, the economy, culture, education and even private life — using propaganda, surveillance and terror against dissidents, as well as bans on parties and ideologies other than its own.

questions.prompt: What particularly distinguished Nazi ideology from Italian fascism?
questions.opener: Think about the role that race biology and antisemitism played in each ideology.
choices: Fascism in Italy was built on the same race-biological antisemitism as Nazism from the start

Nazism was built on a race-biological ideology with extreme antisemitism as a central part, while Italian fascism was primarily built on ultranationalism and a cult of the leader without the same race-biological core
Nazism and fascism had no common features at all
Fascism rejected all forms of nationalism
questions.explanation: Both Nazism and fascism were totalitarian and ultranationalist and built on a strong cult of the leader, but Nazism had a race-biological core with extreme antisemitism as a central part of the ideology, which was not as central to Italian fascism from the start.

questions.prompt: Which event meant that the war in Europe became a world war in the true sense, by drawing in the USA as well?
questions.opener: Think about a Japanese attack on an American naval base in the Pacific in December 1941.
choices: The Battle of Stalingrad
The invasion of Poland in 1939
Japan's attack on the American naval base Pearl Harbor in December 1941
The Munich Agreement of 1938
questions.explanation: Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 led the USA to formally enter the war, against both Japan and Nazi Germany. The war thereby truly became global, with fighting in Europe, North Africa and the Pacific.

questions.opener: Think of a systematic, industrially organised genocide aimed at a specific group of people.
choices: Nazi Germany's systematic, industrially organised genocide of around six million Jews, along with the persecution of Roma, disabled people and other groups
A series of battles between Germany and the Soviet Union over territory
A peace treaty that ended the Second World War
An economic crisis in Germany during the 1920s
questions.explanation: The Holocaust was Nazi Germany's systematic murder of around six million Jews, carried out with industrial organisation in concentration and extermination camps. Roma, disabled people, political opponents and other groups were also persecuted and murdered.

questions.prompt: Compare the League of Nations (founded after the First World War) with the UN (founded after the Second World War). Why did one succeed better than the other at preserving peace?
questions.opener: Think about which countries were involved, and what means of power the organisation had.
questions.answer: The UN was built with lessons learned from the League of Nations' weaknesses: more great powers were involved from the start (including the USA and the Soviet Union), and the Security Council was given the ability to decide on collective, including military, action against aggressors, which gave the organisation greater weight — even though the UN too has not been able to prevent every conflict.
steps: The League of Nations was founded in 1920 to prevent new wars, but the USA never joined, which weakened the organisation from the start.
The League lacked its own means of power to stop aggressors, which became clear when Japan invaded Manchuria and Italy attacked Ethiopia without real consequences.
The UN was founded in 1945 having learned from this: all the great powers, including the USA and the Soviet Union, became members from the start.
The UN Security Council was given the authority to decide on sanctions and military action against states that threaten peace.
Despite this, the veto power of the five permanent members has sometimes left the UN paralysed, so the organisation has not been able to prevent every conflict since 1945.

questions.prompt: Summarise the world wars of the 20th century: causes, ideologies, course of events and consequences.
questions.opener: Two wars, totalitarian ideologies, a genocide and a new world order.
questions.answer: The First World War (1914–1918) was triggered by the assassination in Sarajevo but was rooted in militarism, imperialism and the alliance system · the Second World War (1939–1945) was driven by Nazi German and Japanese expansionist ambitions and began when Germany invaded Poland · totalitarian ideologies such as Nazism, fascism and Stalinist communism sought to control the whole of society, with propaganda and terror · the Holocaust was Nazi Germany's systematic genocide of around six million Jews and the persecution of other groups · turning points such as the Battle of Stalingrad and the Allied landings in Normandy turned the fortunes of war against Germany · the war ended in 1945 with the defeat of Germany and Japan, following the atomic bombs over Hiroshima and Nagasaki · the UN was founded in 1945 to, having learned from the failure of the League of Nations, better preserve international peace.

questions.prompt: What did the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 mean for Germany?
questions.opener: Think about guilt, money, territory and the military in the terms of the peace.
choices: Germany was forced to accept blame for the war, pay heavy war reparations, cede territory and drastically limit its military
Germany was allowed to keep all its colonies and its full military power
Germany was rewarded with new territory for its war effort
The peace contained no economic or territorial demands on Germany
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 forced Germany to formally accept blame for the war, pay heavy war reparations, cede territory and colonies, and drastically limit its military. The harsh terms contributed to the widespread discontent that Nazism was later able to exploit politically.

questions.prompt: How did Adolf Hitler and the Nazi party come to power in Germany in 1933?
questions.opener: Think about whether it was a direct armed seizure of power, or a process through elections and appointments.
choices: Through a combination of democratic elections, political alliances and Hitler's appointment as chancellor, after which democracy was rapidly dismantled
Through an armed military coup against the government
Through a foreign invasion that installed Hitler in power
Through a direct decision by the League of Nations
questions.explanation: The Nazi party achieved major electoral successes in the early 1930s, and President Hindenburg appointed Hitler as chancellor in January 1933 after political negotiations and alliances with conservative forces. The Enabling Act that same year then allowed Hitler to rapidly dismantle the democratic order.

questions.opener: Think about which major landing opened a new front in the west against Nazi Germany.
choices: The Allies' major landing in Normandy in France, which opened a western front against Nazi Germany
Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union
Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor
The end of the Battle of Stalingrad
questions.explanation: D-Day on 6 June 1944 was the Western Allies' major landing in Normandy in northern France, which opened a decisive western front against Nazi Germany and contributed greatly to Germany's final defeat less than a year later.

questions.prompt: Why is the Battle of Stalingrad (1942–1943) usually seen as a turning point on the Eastern Front?
questions.opener: Think about which side went from attacking to being able to launch a counteroffensive after the battle.
choices: The German defeat meant the German army's offensive strength on the Eastern Front was broken, and the Soviet Union could subsequently launch a counteroffensive
It was the only battle of the entire war
Germany won a decisive victory that prolonged the war
The battle took place in Berlin
questions.explanation: The German defeat at Stalingrad, in which an entire German army was destroyed or captured, broke the German army's offensive strength on the Eastern Front. After this, the Soviet Union was able to gradually go on the counteroffensive and push the German army back towards Berlin.

questions.prompt: What was the Wannsee Conference of 1942?
questions.opener: Think of a meeting where the practical logistics of a mass murder were planned.
choices: Senior Nazi officials coordinated the practical organisation of the 'Final Solution', the systematic extermination of Europe's Jews
A peace meeting between the Allies and Germany
A meeting at which Hitler resigned as leader
A conference on Germany's economic reconstruction
questions.explanation: At the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, senior Nazi officials coordinated the bureaucratic and logistical organisation of the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question' — the systematic genocide that later came to be called the Holocaust.

questions.prompt: Who are the UN Security Council's five permanent members, each of whom has veto power?
questions.opener: Think about which great powers were the victorious powers after the Second World War.
choices: The USA, Russia (formerly the Soviet Union), China, Britain and France
The USA, Germany, Japan, Italy and China
All UN member states rotate as permanent members
Only the USA and the Soviet Union/Russia
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council's five permanent members — the USA, Russia (which succeeded the Soviet Union's seat), China, Britain and France — were the leading victorious powers after the Second World War, and each of them has veto power over Security Council decisions.

questions.prompt: What was the policy of appeasement that Britain and France pursued towards Nazi Germany up to 1939?
questions.opener: Think about how the Western powers reacted to Germany's demands for the Sudetenland in 1938.
choices: A policy of concessions that accepted German territorial demands (e.g. the Sudetenland in 1938) in the hope of avoiding a new major war
A policy that meant an immediate declaration of war on Germany as early as 1935
A trade embargo against Germany from 1933
Military cooperation with Nazi Germany against the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: The policy of appeasement meant that Britain and France made concessions to Nazi Germany's territorial demands, for example through the Munich Agreement of 1938, which gave Germany the Sudetenland, in the hope of avoiding a new major war. The policy failed when Germany continued to expand and eventually invaded Poland in 1939.
